title: Development of machine learning algorithms to predict achievement of minimal clinically important difference for the KOOS‐PS following total knee arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: stochastic gradient boosting, random forest, support vector machine, neural network, elastic-net penalized logistic regression
prom_instruments: KOOS-PS, PROMIS Global PF, PROMIS Global MH, VAS Pain
notes: MCID calculated via distribution-based method (0.5 SD of preoperative-to-postoperative change). 28.9% missing 1-year postoperative KOOS handled via multiple imputation (missForest). Only internal validation performed; authors acknowledge lack of external validation as a limitation. 72.8% of patients achieved MCID. Model deployed as open-access web application at https://sorg-apps.shinyapps.io/tka_koos_mcid/. Cross-validation also performed on training set (10-fold, repeated 3 times). Study conducted at 2 academic and 3 community medical centers in the USA.

title: Surgical factors play a critical role in predicting functional outcomes using machine learning in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: L2-penalised logistic regression (ridge), support vector machine, random forest, CatBoost, dummy classifier
prom_instruments: KOOS JR, WOMAC Function, WOMAC Pain
notes: Study population restricted to robotic-assisted TKA (Mako, Stryker) from two surgeons at a single US center; two authors are Stryker employees and one is a Stryker consultant/sponsored researcher, representing significant conflict of interest. Patients with BMI>=40 or age>=89 were excluded, limiting generalizability. No external validation performed; authors acknowledge need for multicenter validation. Sample size (n=423, with subsets of 344-385 per PROM) may be underpowered for the number of features tested. Nested cross-validation with 80/20 train-test split used; n_train and n_test are approximate (80% of ~423). The target class was 'no MCID' (not achieving MCID), which differs from most literature predicting MCID achievement, complicating direct comparison. Three separate models built for three PROMs with three feature sets each (9 model configurations per algorithm). Best AUC of 0.80 reported for WOMAC Function with ridge logistic regression; KOOS JR best AUC was 0.75 with CatBoost; WOMAC Pain best AUC was 0.79 with CatBoost. F1 scores were low (0.44-0.62), reflecting class imbalance. Imaging features derived from preoperative CT scan and intraoperative robotic system data.

title: Machine learning algorithms do not outperform preoperative thresholds in predicting clinically meaningful improvements after total knee arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression with L1-regularization (LASSO)
best_algorithm: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) for SF-36 PCS; XGB/SVM tied for SF-36 MCS; RF/LASSO tied for WOMAC
notes: Study prospectively collected registry data from a single institution in Singapore (2008-2018). 85.4% follow-up rate at 2 years. Class imbalance handled via random oversampling. Hyperparameter tuning via 5-fold cross-validation on training set only; final evaluation on held-out test set. Missing data imputed with median values (BMI n=9, preop pain score n=5). No external validation. Key finding: ML did not outperform simple preoperative PROM thresholds. Permutation importance used for interpretability. Brier score reported as a calibration-adjacent metric but formal calibration plots not shown. Only top 2 ML models per outcome reported in results table. The best AUC of 0.95 was for SF-36 MCS prediction (XGB and SVM tied); WOMAC best was 0.89 (RF and LASSO tied); SF-36 PCS best was 0.77 (XGB). Sensitivity and specificity values reported correspond to the WOMAC threshold model for illustration in text.

title: The utility of machine learning algorithms for the prediction of patient-reported outcome measures following primary hip and knee total joint arthroplasty
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
ml_algorithms: Artificial Neural Network, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, Elastic-Net Penalized Logistic Regression
prom_instruments: HOOS-PS, KOOS-PS, Physical Function SF10A, PROMIS SF Physical, PROMIS SF Mental
notes: Study uses 80:20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation on training set; no external validation cohort. Multiple PROMs predicted but outcome binarization threshold not explicitly described. Female percentage not directly reported (THA: 1094 females/2137=51.2%; TKA: 1118 females/2389=46.8%; combined ~48.8%). Mean age reported as combined 71.8 years. Indication stated as end-stage osteoarthritis but not formally labeled. AUC >0.83 across all models; best AUC 0.87 for ANN on both THA and TKA test sets. Models predicted PROM scores within 1.5 points of actual in 96.6% THA and 96.1% TKA cases. Single tertiary academic center limits generalizability. Most patient factors were binary, limiting assessment of disease severity gradients.

title: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of lower limb muscle mass and fatty degeneration in patients with knee osteoarthritis and its correlation with Knee Society Score
journal: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery
ml_algorithms: Bayesian U-Net (deep learning-based AI segmentation)
other_metric_value: rho up to 0.53 (gluteus medius/minimus vs functional activities); Dice 0.958
notes: This study uses AI (Bayesian U-Net) primarily as a segmentation tool to extract imaging features (muscle volume and CT attenuation/HU values) from preoperative CT scans, not as a predictive ML model for PROMs per se. The statistical analysis relating these features to KSS is conventional (Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression), not ML-based prediction. The PROM (KSS) was measured preoperatively (cross-sectional study), not postoperatively. Sample size is very small (n=43) limiting multivariate analysis. Cross-validation (n=34) was only for AI segmentation accuracy, not for the regression model predicting KSS. No missing data handling described for regression. Predominantly female cohort (79%). Study may not strictly qualify as an ML-for-PROM-prediction study in the traditional sense — human review recommended for inclusion/exclusion decision.

title: IMU-augmented Patient-related Outcome Measure for Knee Arthroplasty Patients
journal: Journal of Medical and Biological Engineering
ml_algorithms: Linear Regression, Random Forest Regression
notes: Very small sample (n=28, including 5 UKR patients who are not TKA); study includes unicompartmental knee replacement (UKR) patients alongside TKA. R2>0.90 refers to KCF prediction from IMUs, not PROM prediction. PROM prediction performance reported as MAE margin (1.81-4.40 units of EQ-5D-5L VAS at 95% CI). Temporal cross-validation used (80/20 split per participant). Outliers excluded from some analyses. Very small sample size relative to number of features raises overfitting concerns. Multiple timepoints analysed (physio sessions, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year). Best model varied by timepoint. Study is primarily a feasibility/pilot study with acknowledged need for more data.

title: Deep learning−based clustering for endotyping and post-arthroplasty response classification using knee osteoarthritis multiomic data
ml_algorithms: variational autoencoder (omicVAE), K-means clustering, logistic regression, lasso regression, ridge regression, support vector machines, random forests, Naive Bayes meta-classifier
best_algorithm: Integrative framework: random forests (unimodal) + Naive Bayes meta-classifier (multimodal)
other_metric: AUC per cluster (pain: cluster 1=0.841, cluster 2=0.816, cluster 3=0.879; function: cluster 1=0.786, cluster 2=0.808, cluster 3=0.738)
other_metric_value: pain cluster 3 integrative AUC=0.879; function cluster 2 integrative AUC=0.808
notes: Study uses multiomic data (miRNomics and metabolomics from plasma, synovial fluid, urine) rather than standard clinical predictors. Primary aim is endotyping via unsupervised deep learning (omicVAE + K-means), with secondary supervised ML for WOMAC pain/function responder classification within each cluster. No external validation cohort; authors acknowledge this limitation. Feature types are molecular omics (miRNA + metabolites), not standard clinical/imaging features. Responder threshold defined as >33% improvement in WOMAC pain or function. Clusters did not differ significantly in pain/function outcomes, limiting clinical interpretability of endotypes for outcome prediction. Sample size of 414 with up to 2727 features raises overfitting concerns despite 10-fold cross-validation. Code and data publicly available on GitHub and GEO (GSE222979). PROBAST D4 rated high risk due to very high feature-to-sample ratio and no external validation.

title: Development of Machine Learning Algorithms to Predict Clinically Meaningful Improvement for the Patient-Reported Health State After Total Hip Arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: stochastic gradient boosting, random forest, support vector machine, neural network, elastic net penalized logistic regression
prom_instruments: EQ-5D PRHS (patient-reported health state), modified Harris Hip Score
notes: MCID calculated using distribution-based method (0.5 SD of postoperative PRHS), not anchor-based; median age reported rather than mean; BMI reported as median (IQR) not mean; no external validation performed — authors acknowledge this limitation; 80:20 train-test split with cross-validation on training set only; ROM excluded due to >30% missingness; multiple imputation used for remaining missing data; open-access Shiny app deployed for clinical use; sample size of 616 may be modest for 5 algorithms with 8 features but internal validation performed; calibration slope of 1.45 for best model suggests some miscalibration.

title: Can Machine Learning Methods Produce Accurate and Easy-to-Use Preoperative Prediction Models of One-Year Improvements in Pain and Functioning After Knee Arthroplasty?
ml_algorithms: logistic regression, LASSO regression, gradient boosting machines, quadratic discriminant analysis
prom_instruments: KOOS, KOOS JR, KOOS Pain, KOOS Symptoms, KOOS ADL, KOOS Recreation, KOOS QoL
notes: Study population is predominantly male (93.2%) US veterans from VA healthcare system; authors explicitly caution that external validation is needed before use in general arthroplasty population. MCID thresholds were determined using Youden Index anchor-based method with SAPS satisfaction as anchor. Best C-statistic was 0.76 for KOOS ADL (logistic regression); models for KOOS JR and Recreation subscales performed poorly (C-statistic ≤0.60). No external validation performed. Sensitivity/specificity values reported are for a 0.4 probability threshold for KOOS Symptoms scale as an example. Bootstrap and 10-fold cross-validation both used for internal validation. Models described as freely available from authors.

title: Natural Language Processing of Patient-Experience Comments After Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: Natural Language Processing (sentiment analysis)
prom_instruments: KOOS Jr, Numeric Pain Rating Scale
other_metric: agreement rate between automated and manual sentiment classification
notes: This study uses NLP primarily for sentiment classification of free-text patient comments, not for predicting PROMs in the traditional sense. The primary outcome is sentiment of patient comments (negative vs non-negative), with KOOS Jr and pain scores used as secondary comparators between groups. NLP was vendor-supplied (Press Ganey Associates), not developed by authors. Only ~50% of TKA patients completed the survey, introducing significant nonresponse bias. PROM follow-up is only 6 weeks. Study does not predict PROMs using ML in the conventional sense — it uses NLP to classify comment sentiment and then compares PROMs between groups. This paper may be only marginally relevant to a systematic review on ML prediction of PROMs after TKA/THA. Manual review confirmed 96.3% agreement with automated NLP classification. No formal ML model validation performed.

title: Patient Factors That Matter in Predicting Hip Arthroplasty Outcomes: A Machine-Learning Approach
ml_algorithms: LASSO
notes: Small sample (n=160) with 20+ predictors raises overfitting concerns; cross-validated R2 mean was only 10% (SD=7%, range 0-38%), substantially lower than full-sample R2 of 31%, indicating likely optimism. LASSO used for variable selection and regression in same dataset without separate holdout. Follow-up at 3 months is short and variable (mean 126 days, SD 119 days, range 33-458 days). Baseline HOOS excluded from model due to collinearity. Listwise deletion used for missing data. Bootstrapping of coefficients conducted (1000 iterations). Model described as predictive rather than causal. Only one ML algorithm (LASSO) tested. Study is primarily a feature-selection/regression exercise rather than a traditional ML classification study.

title: Logistic Regression and Machine Learning Models Cannot Discriminate Between Satisfied and Dissatisfied Total Knee Arthroplasty Patients
ml_algorithms: logistic regression, elastic net logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosted trees, extreme gradient boosted trees, support vector machines, neural networks
notes: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data. No ML model outperformed logistic regression (AUC 0.736). All models had low sensitivity (0.083-0.44) and poor kappa scores, suggesting limited clinical utility as discriminatory tools. Authors note sample size likely too small for optimal ML model development. Missing data handled via k-nearest neighbors imputation; several KSCRS subscales excluded due to >15% missing data. No comorbidity measure included. 70:30 train-test split with stratification used; no cross-validation on test set. Calibration assessed via Brier score and Cox intercept/slope. Corrigendum published correcting Figure 1B axis labels.

title: Coronal and Sagittal Component Position in Contemporary Total Knee Arthroplasty: Targeting Native Alignment Optimizes Clinical Outcomes
ml_algorithms: Classification and Regression Tree (CART)
prom_instruments: KSS, KOOS JR, UCLA Activity Level Score, Likert satisfaction scale
notes: Study uses only 3 radiographic alignment features (PTS change, postoperative TFA, postoperative FF) as inputs to CART models; authors acknowledge sample size is lower than ideal for ML models and data overfitting was apparent in some models; 10-fold cross-validation used; best AUC of 0.76 (test) and 0.88 (train) reported only for the preoperative valgus subgroup achieving all MCIDs; mean AUC across preoperative alignment groups ranged 0.55-0.89; single surgeon single institution limits generalizability; minimum 1-year follow-up with mean 2.4 years; 83% PROM response rate; no external validation performed.

title: Using Unsupervised Machine Learning to Predict Quality of Life After Total Knee Arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: Spectral Clustering
other_metric_value: Cluster 5: 100% met MCID at 3mo and 1y; Cluster 4: 23% at 1y, 100% from 3mo to 1y; Cluster 2: 34% at 3mo; Cluster 1 and 3: 0% at 1y
notes: Unsupervised clustering study (spectral clustering); no predictive model built — clusters described post-hoc for clinical interpretation only. Only 36% of eligible patients (636/1737) had complete data, raising substantial selection/sampling bias concerns. No train-test split or internal validation performed. Study cannot predict individual patient outcomes. PROMIS GH-P ceiling effect noted by authors for higher-functioning patients. Single-center Canadian cohort limits generalizability. Indication inferred as OA based on context (knee OA population) though not explicitly stated as exclusively OA. n_features_input estimated from variables used in clustering (age, gender, BMI, FCI comorbidity items, pain score, PROMIS GH-P preop). TRIPOD not formally assessed. No supervised ML comparison performed.

title: Can a Large Language Model Interpret Data in the Electronic Health Record to Infer Minimum Clinically Important Difference Achievement of Knee Osteoarthritis Outcome Score—Joint Replacement Score Following Total Knee Arthroplasty?
ml_algorithms: Large Language Model (ChatGPT 3.5)
notes: Pilot case-control study with only 80 patients (40 MCID achieved, 40 not), balanced by design. Uses ChatGPT 3.5 (general-purpose LLM, not fine-tuned) on manually de-identified EHR notes. LLM was not trained on this task. Notes provided to LLM were limited to orthopaedic, primary care, and ED notes from restricted time windows due to HIPAA constraints. No formal ML training/validation split — LLM used zero-shot. Surgeon comparison included as human baseline. VA population may limit generalizability. No demographic data (age, sex, BMI) reported. Study is explicitly described as a proof-of-concept pilot. Two cases excluded from comparative analysis due to ChatGPT non-response. High risk of bias in D1 (case-control selection), D2 (post-hoc prompt design, no pre-specified feature set), and D4 (very small sample, no internal validation, no overfitting correction).

title: Correlation between Harris hip score and gait analysis through artificial intelligence pose estimation in patients after total hip arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: Principal Component Analysis, K-means clustering, Random Forest
notes: Very small sample (n=51 after exclusions from 65); one k-means cluster excluded due to n=1; postoperative follow-up timepoint not specified; patient demographics (age, sex, BMI) not reported; HHS used as both a PROM and a clinician-administered score with mixed objectivity; gait data collected via AI camera (pose estimation) rather than traditional wearable sensors; training accuracy 75% vs test accuracy 81.8% which may reflect overfitting given tiny test set of 11; indication for THA not clearly specified; inconsistent timing of open pose evaluation across participants noted as limitation.

title: Medium-term patient's satisfaction after primary total knee arthroplasty: enhancing prediction for improved care
ml_algorithms: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines
prom_instruments: KSS, SF-12, KOOS-PS, VAS, Satisfaction Likert scale
notes: Small sample size (n=147) with only 17 dissatisfied patients (15% class imbalance); neutral patients (n=34) excluded from ML classification; performance reported only as percentage improvement over baseline rather than standard metrics (AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity); best algorithm not explicitly named but Random Forest inferred from context; two model variants tested: Day-zero (pre/peri-operative features only) and Year-after (including up to 12-month follow-up PROMs); improvement between models not statistically significant (p=0.098); authors acknowledge results should not guide clinical decisions due to small sample.

title: Identifying who are unlikely to benefit from total knee arthroplasty using machine learning models
ml_algorithms: ConvNeXt-Tiny (CNN), XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Multilayer Perceptron, ResNet101, ResNeXt, Vision Transformer
notes: Study used knee-level data (7224 radiographs) from 5720 patients; some patients had bilateral TKA. pct_female derived from 79% male being overweight/obese — actually 79% female (21% male stated). Mean BMI not directly reported but 79% overweight to severely obese. Feature selection not formally performed; 60 clinical features used. Internal validation only via 5-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning; final evaluation on held-out 20% test set. No external validation performed. Best AUC 0.891 for multimodal model predicting KSS MCID at 2 years; clinical-only model AUC 0.888 for same outcome. Sensitivity reported as recall for KSS clinical-data only model (0.744). SHAP and Grad-CAM used for interpretability. Authors note selection bias due to exclusion of patients with prior knee surgery.

title: Can Machine Learning Algorithms Predict Which Patients Will Achieve Minimally Clinically Important Differences From Total Joint Arthroplasty?
ml_algorithms: logistic LASSO, random forest, linear support vector machine
prom_instruments: SF-36 PCS, SF-36 MCS, HOOS JR, KOOS JR
notes: Study includes both THA (n=7239) and TKA (n=6480) patients from a single high-volume US specialty hospital (Hospital for Special Surgery) 2007-2012. Only 44.3% of eligible TJAs joined the registry and 71.5% of those had complete data, introducing potential selection bias toward healthier patients. Mean age reported separately: THA 63 years, TKA 67 years; combined estimate ~65 used. BMI reported separately: THA 28, TKA 30; combined ~29 used. Female percentage: THA 52%, TKA 61%; combined ~56% used. Best AUROC of 0.89 was for SF-36 MCS prediction. Train/test split was 80/20; n_train and n_test are approximate based on total n=13719. Calibration reported but imperfect for most models except SF-36 MCS. No external validation performed though authors published full model parameters to facilitate external testing. Models cannot be applied off-the-shelf without proper testing. D1 rated high risk due to registry participation rate of 44.3% and potential selection bias toward healthier patients.

title: Predicting whether patients will achieve minimal clinically important differences following hip or knee arthroplasty: A performance comparison of machine learning, logistic regression, and pre-surgery PROM scores using data from nine German hospitals
ml_algorithms: artificial neural network, gradient boosting machine, LASSO regression, ridge regression, elastic net, random forest, logistic regression
best_algorithm: varies by outcome: random forest (KA EQ-5D-5L), elastic net (KA EQ-VAS, KA KOOS-PS), gradient boosting machine (HA EQ-5D-5L), LASSO (HA EQ-VAS), ridge regression (HA HOOS-PS)
other_metric: Brier Score, calibration slope, calibration intercept, g-mean, Youden Index
notes: Study uses control group only from an RCT (PROMoting Quality, DRKS00019916); patients who mathematically could not reach MCID were excluded from analysis, which the authors note inflates AUC if not done. Best AUC of 0.84 is for HA EQ-VAS (LASSO). ML significantly outperformed LR in 2/6 cases and pre-surgery PROM scores in 2/6 cases. 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning on training data only. SHAP analysis used for interpretability. Exact n_train and n_test not reported per subsample. Mean age and pct_female are approximate averages across both groups. Indication described as osteoarthritis context but not explicitly stated as inclusion criterion.

title: Computerized adaptive testing for the Oxford Hip, Knee, Shoulder, and Elbow scores: accurate measurement from fewer, and more patient-focused, questions
ml_algorithms: Regression tree learning (CART)
other_metric_value: 0.98 for OHS, OKS, OSS, OES total; 0.95-0.98 for OES subscales
notes: This study is not a standard ML prediction study for postoperative PROMs following TKA/THA. It develops computerized adaptive testing (CAT) algorithms using regression tree learning to estimate full-length PROM scores (OHS, OKS, OSS, OES) from fewer items. The study includes both preoperative and postoperative responses mixed together; it does not predict postoperative outcomes from preoperative features. The OKS and OHS test sets include arthroplasty patients but the study is not specifically a TKA/THA outcome prediction study. n_total, n_tka, n_tha refer to test set sizes for OKS and OHS respectively; total patients across all instruments in test sets is 11,738. Training set totals: OHS 5000, OKS 9484, OSS 2258, OES 8359. Mean age not reported as a single figure; median ages by instrument range from 56-68 years. Percentage female not reported as a single figure. Funded by Universal Research Solutions LLC (commercial conflict of interest). This paper likely falls outside the scope of a systematic review focused on ML prediction of PROMs following TKA/THA.

title: Prediction of quality-of-life improvement after total hip arthroplasty: A simplified and internally validated model based on 82,526 total hip arthroplasties from the Swedish Arthroplasty Register
ml_algorithms: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, Ridge Regression, Lasso Regression, Logistic Regression, Classification Tree, Classification Tree with Pruning
notes: Large national registry study (n=82,526 THAs from Swedish Arthroplasty Register 2000-2018). Five outcomes predicted using two MCID thresholds for EQ-5D (SRM=0.196 and CoB=0.428) and one for EQ-VAS (7.81). AUC range 0.80-0.97 across outcomes; best AUC 0.97 for EQ-5D CoB threshold with GBM. Pct female calculated from 43.3% male reported. Missing data handled by complete-case analysis (exclusion), not imputation — authors acknowledge this may introduce bias. Possible dependency between baseline EQ-5D and MCID-defined outcome (floor effect/regression to mean). No external validation performed; authors recommend future validation on NJR. PROBAST D2 flagged: preoperative PROMs used as predictors but are also components of the outcome calculation, raising potential data leakage concern. PROBAST D4 flagged: no calibration reported, no correction for optimism beyond train-test split, missing data handled by exclusion only. Mean BMI not reported as a single value; BMI provided as categorical distribution only. Mean age 67.9 years from Table I (full SAR extract before final cleaning, n=154,595); may differ slightly for final n=82,526 cohort.

title: Kinematic alignment in total knee arthroplasty: a five-year prospective, multicentre, survivorship study
notes: This paper is NOT an AI/ML study and does not belong in a systematic review of ML for predicting PROMs. It is a prospective clinical outcomes study of kinematic alignment TKA using image-derived instrumentation, reporting PROM improvements and survivorship at 5 years. No machine learning or predictive modeling was performed. All ML-related fields are left empty. Flagged for exclusion from the systematic review.

title: Improved Prediction of Postoperative Knee Function Using Preoperative Patient Factors and Intraoperative Measures of Bony Resection, Ligament Release, and Implant Alignment in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Database Analysis of 363 Cases
ml_algorithms: Linear Regression, Support Vector Machine, XGBoost
other_metric: Percentage of patients with OKS correctly predicted within MICD
notes: Small single-center sample (n=363) with no external validation; authors acknowledge this limitation explicitly. Intraoperative navigation data included as predictors alongside preoperative clinical factors, which is a novel feature. Models explain only 29-37% of variance in postoperative OKS. Patients with lowest OKS values were systematically predicted to have much better outcomes (regression to the mean issue). No demographic summary statistics (mean age, BMI, sex distribution) reported in the abstract or results. Conference proceedings paper — limited methodological detail. Missing data handling not described. R2=0.37 for best model (linear regression) on validation set.

title: Predictive Model and Web-based Calculator for the Oxford Hip Score After Total Hip Replacement
ml_algorithms: Radial Basis Function Kernel Regularized Least Squares, Linear Regression with Backwards Selection, Linear Regression with Forward Selection, Principal Component Analysis, Support Vector Machines with Linear Kernel, Random Forest, Neural Network, Recursive Partitioning, Stochastic Gradient Boosting, Boosted Generalized Linear Model, Bagged Model, k-Nearest Neighbors, Sparse Partial Least Squares, Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines
notes: Study uses NHS PROMs/HES national registry from England 2010-2015. Total eligible was 192,514; 21,300 excluded for age <50, leaving 171,214. R-squared of 0.18 is low, suggesting limited predictive accuracy despite large sample. Missing data handled via k-nearest neighbors imputation. 5-fold cross-validation used. Web-based calculator developed and publicly available. Authors claim 'highly accurate models' but R2=0.18 contradicts this. Paper states results are 'representative of the entire US population' which appears to be an error as data is from England. No external validation performed. Number of input features not explicitly stated. BMI not reported in sample characteristics.

title: Modeling to Predict the Patients' Postoperative WOMAC Score by Features Engineering and Gradient Boost Tree
journal: Suranaree Journal of Science and Technology
ml_algorithms: Generalized Linear Model, Support Vector Machine, Deep Learning, Gradient Boost Tree
best_algorithm: Gradient Boost Tree with FE+GBT attributes
notes: Data collected from a single hospital (Suranaree University of Technology Hospital) between 2007-2018. No demographic breakdown (age, sex, BMI distributions) reported beyond attribute ranges. Postoperative follow-up timepoint not specified. Only 12 attributes used from original 21; feature engineering used to select/generate new attributes. No external validation performed; only 10-fold cross-validation. Sample size of 1250 with up to 11 input features is reasonable but overfitting risk not formally assessed. WOMAC score range in dataset reported as 15.2-100 (expected 0-96), suggesting possible data quality issue. No missing data handling strategy described. Journal is a regional Thai science journal; DOI not provided in text.

title: Role of AI in the analysis of total knee arthroplasty
ml_algorithms: ChatGPT (generative language model)
notes: Study uses ChatGPT (a general-purpose generative language model, not a trained ML model) as the predictive tool by submitting structured patient data via prompt engineering — this is a highly unconventional and methodologically weak approach. No formal model training, cross-validation, or internal validation was performed. Sample size of 98 is very small. KOOS outcomes were surgeon-reported rather than patient-reported, raising concerns about outcome measurement validity. AUC of 0.70 reported for infection prediction but only 1-2 infection events observed (1.8% of 98), making ROC analysis unreliable. Pearson r=0.45 for KOOS regression. No missing data handling described. No feature selection. Single-center, single-country study. Results should be interpreted with extreme caution. High risk of bias across all PROBAST domains.
